E.definition: It states that a collection of point charges cannot be maintained in a stable static equilibrium configuration solely by the electrostatic interaction of the charges. This theorem was first proved by Samuel Earnshaw in 1842 and it is a fundamental result concerning bodies that interact according to inverse square laws, such as Coulomb's law of electrostatics and Newton's law of gravitation. It applies to the classical law forces (electric and gravitational) and also to the magnetic forces of permanent magnets and paramagnetic materials but not diamagnetic materials.

The theorem, named after William Frederick Eberlein and Witold Lwowitsch Schmulian that asserts the equivalence of compactness (Heine-Borel compactness), sequential compactness and limit point compactness in the weak topology for a Banach space.

The ratio of the elevation of the boiling point of a solvent caused by dissolving a solute to the molality of the solution, taken at extremely low concentrations and relates molality to boiling point elevation. Its symbol is Kb.

A mathematical model of an economic system in which, commonly, there are m producers, each with a production set P j and n consumers, each with a consumption set C i and an associated ordering ≤ i . These sets lie on an Euclidean space, whose dimension corresponds to the number of goods in the economy. There is a total resource level w . The producers each produce a vector y i in P j and the consumers have a demand x i in C i . These m + n elements define a state of the economy. The excess demand is ∑ x i - ∑ y j - w and a market equilibrium occurs if excess demand is zero. Individual consumers will try to maximize their preference satisfaction; this leads to the study of equilibria that occur as a market equilibrium together with a pricing of resources that every producer maximizes profit and every consumer optimizes satisfaction.

A theoretical limit for the maximum value of the brightness of a star of a given E mass, named after British astronomer and physicist, Arthur Stanley Eddington and given as L = 4 π GMm p c σ T , where G is the gravitational pressure, M is the mass of the luminous object, m P is the mass of a proton, c is the speed of light and σ T is the effective area of an electron when it is illuminated by radiation. This limit exists because the radiation pressure caused by the nuclear fission reactions powering the star has to counter, but not exceed the gravitational force that would cause gravitational collapse of the star. A star emitting radiation at greater than the Eddington limit would break up. In a star it is defined as the point where the gravitational force inwards equals the continuum radiation force outwards, assuming hydrostatic equilibrium and spherical symmetry. When exceeding the Eddington luminosity, a star would initiate a very intense continuum driven stellar wind from its outer layers. Since most massive stars have luminosities far below the Eddington limit, however, their winds are mostly driven by the less intense line absorption.

The apparent nuclear or net positive charge which an outermost electron actually experiences through attraction in a multi-electron atom as a result of the shielding effect by other electrons. Its symbol is Z eff . Since the shielding effect of negatively charged electrons prevents higher orbital electrons from experiencing the full nuclear charge by the repelling effect of inner- layered electrons, the term 'effective' is used to qualify the nuclear charge. The strength of the nuclear charge can be determined by looking at the oxidation number of the atom. Where there is only one electron in an atom, that electron experiences the full charge of the positive nucleus, in which case, the effective nuclear charge can be calculated from Coulomb's law. However, in a multi-electron atom the outer electrons are simultaneously attracted to the positive nucleus E and repelled by the negatively charged electrons. The effective nuclear charge on such an electron is given by the expression: Z eff = Z - S, where, Z is the number of protons in the nucleus (atomic number) and S is the average number of electrons between the nucleus and the electron in question (the number of nonvalence electrons).

1. A measure of the performance or how well a machine or other energy changing device changes energy into useful work. It is the measure of the percentage ratio of work output to work input. For a simple machine, it is given by: E = Energy Output Energy input × 100%. For example, a gear transmission is 97% efficient, when the useful energy output is 97% of the input, with the other 3% being lost as heat due to friction. Automobile engines have low efficiency (below 30%) because out of the total energy content of fuel converted to heat, only a small portion provides motive power, while a substantial amount is lost in the radiator and car exhaust. 2. In chemistry, it is the ratio between the useful energy delivered or bound and the energy supplied: energy output/energy input. It is also used in the sense of a quantitative measure of the relative rate of a given step involving a species with respect to the sum of the rates of all of the parallel steps which depopulate that species. Its symbol is η.
The force given to a machine to move a load and expressed as: Effort = Load (Force)/Distance.

The theorem that a quantum-mechanical wave packet obeys the equations of motion of the corresponding classical particle when the position, momentum and force acting on the particle are replaced by the expectation values of these quantities.

Eigenvalue equations appear in many contexts, including the solution of systems of linear algebraic equations (matrix equations), differential or partial differential equations and integral equations. Alternatively, it is defined as the relationship E max = hf - W , where E max is the maximum kinetic energy of electrons emitted in the photo-emissive effect; h , the Planck's constant; f , the frequency of the incident radiation and W the work function of the emitter. 2. Einstein's Field Equations (EFE) or Einstein's equations are a set of ten equations in Albert Einstein's theory of general relativity which describe the fundamental interaction of gravitation as a result of space-time being curved by matter and energy. Apart from obeying local energy-momentum conservation, the EFE reduces to Newton's law of gravitation, where the gravitational field is weak and velocities much less than the speed of light. In much the same way that electromagnetic fields are determined (using charges and currents via Maxwell's equations) the EFE is used to determine the space-time geometry resulting from the presence of mass-energy and linear momentum relationship between the metric tensor and the Einstein tensor and it allows the EFE to be written as a set of non-linear partial differential equations when used in this way. The solutions of the EFE are the components of the metric tensor. These equations are also used to study phenomena such as gravitational waves. Also, special classes of exact solutions are most often studied because they model many gravitational phenomena, such as rotating black holes and the expanding universe.

German-born American physicist and Nobel laureate, who is best known as the creator of the special and general theories of relativity and for his hypothesis concerning the particle nature of light. In 1905, he published three papers, each of which had a profound effect on the development of physics. In one paper, he proposed the theory of special relativity, which provides a correct description for particles travelling at high speeds. The two postulates of the special theory of relativity were that the speed of light in a vacuum is constant and that the laws of physics are the same for all inertial reference frames. He is best known for his mass-energy equivalence formula $$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$E = mc^2$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$ . He received the1921 Nobel Prize in Physics "for his services to theoretical physics and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect". He is probably the most well known scientist of the 20 th century.

An unexpected connection revealed independently by Albert Einstein in 1905 and Marian Smoluchowski in 1906 in their papers on Brownian motion, which is a relationship between the diffusion coefficient D and the distance λ that a particle can jump in a time τ . The equation is given as D = λ 2 /2 τ and it gives a connection between the microscopic details of particle diffusion and the macroscopic quantities associated with the diffusion. This equation is an early example of a fluctuation-dissipation relation and it is frequently used in the electro diffusion phenomena.

A condition that is sufficient for a polynomial with integer coefficients to be irreducible. It states that it suffices to find a prime p that does not divide the leading coefficient of the polynomial and that does divide all other coefficients, but is such that p 2 does not divide the constant coefficient. For example, the polynomial x n^-3 is irreducible for all n , but x n^-9 need not be. The corresponding result holds in a principal ideal domain. The criterion E is named after German mathematician, Ferdinand Gotthold Max Eisenstein (1823-1852).
The reciprocal of capacitance (ability to store electric charge). It is measured in farad^-1 .

The ratio of the stress applied to a body to the strain produced or the slope of its stress-strain curve in the elastic deformation region. It is the mathematical description of an object's tendency to be deformed elastically, when a force is applied to it. It may be expressed as λ = stress strain , where λ (lambda) is the elastic modulus, stress the force causing the deformation divided by the area to which the force is applied and strain, the ratio of the change caused by the stress to the original state of the object. If stress is measured in pascals, since strain is a unitless ratio, then the units of λ are also pascals. Due to the fact that the denominator of the above equation becomes unity if length is doubled, the elastic modulus becomes the stress needed to cause a sample of the material to double in length. Since this endpoint is not realistic because most materials will fail before reaching it, it is practical, due to the fact that small fractions of the defining load will operate in the same ratio.

The fundamental property of matter that allows one object to exert an electric force on another object when near each other without physically touching. The amount of electric charge is defined by the word equation, electric charge ( Q ) = current ( I ) × time ( t in seconds). The SI unit of electric charge is the coulomb ( C ). It occurs in nature in two forms and conventionally described as positive and negative in order to distinguish between them in terms of the kinds of interactions they can have. The proton has a positive charge and the electron has a negative charge is a property of the electron. Two positively or negatively charged substances experience a mutual repulsive force, while positively charged objects and negatively charged objects experience an attractive force.

The absolute permittivity of empty space, with the symbol ε 0 . It is equal to 1 in centimetre-gram-second electrostatic units and to farads per metre, where c o is the speed of light in free space and μ 0 is the vacuum permeability). Numerically, it is equal to 8.854 × 10 -12 farad per metre.

A measure of the density of an electric current, defined as a vector whose magnitude is the electric current per cross-sectional area. In SI units, the current density is measured in amperes per square metre. Its symbol is J . By magnitude it is the electric current divided by the cross sectional area: J = I / A , where I is the current flowing through the conductor given in Amperes and A is the cross sectional area in m2 .

The charge per unit area that would be displaced across a layer of a conductor placed across an electric field. Its symbol is D and it stands for displacement. The electric displacement field D is, therefore, defined as D ≡ ε 0 E + P , where ε 0 is the permittivity in free space, E is the actual average value of the electric field and P is the (macroscopic) density of the permanent and induced electric dipole moments in the material, known as the polarisation density. It is a vector field whose divergence depends on the density of bound charge in the material. It is responsible for the effects of free charges within materials. In free space, the electric displacement field is equivalent to flux density, a concept that lends understanding to Gauss's law.

A region within which a particle possessing electric charge experiences a force owing to the distribution of other charges; or a region around an electric charge in which an electric force is exerted on another charge. Its strength, E at any point is defined as the electric force , F exerted per unit positive electric charge, Q at that point: E = F Q . It is a type of electromagnetic field, having both magnitude and direction and can be represented by lines of force or field lines, that start on positive charges and terminate on negative charges. The electric field is stronger, where the field lines are closer than where they are farther apart. The value of the electric field has dimensions of force per unit charge and is measured in units of newtons per coulomb.

A vector quantity, which is a measure of the strength of an electric field at a given point in space. It is equal to the force the field would induce on a unit electric charge at that point. Its symbol is E with a standard unit of volt per metre (v/m or v m^-1 ) or newton/coulomb: Force (newton)/Charge (coulomb): Its strength, E at any point is defined as the electric force F exerted per unit positive electric charge Q at that point: E = F Q . The fiel d strength E at a point is defined as the force per unit charge acting on a small positive charge placed at the point. The field strength at a particular distance from an object is directly proportional to the electric charge (in coulombs) on that object and inversely proportional to the distance from a charged object.

The strength of electric field acting on a particular area, defined as the area size multiplied by the component of the field acting at right angles to the area, expressed as ∅ = EA , where ∅ (phi) is the electric flux, E is the strength of the electric field and A is the area size.

The vector field that expresses the density of permanent or induced electric dipole moments in a dielectric material or slight relative shift of positive and negative electric charge in opposite directions within an insulator or dielectric, induced by an external electric field. It occurs when an electric field distorts the negative cloud of electrons around positive atomic nuclei in a direction opposite the field. The polarisation vector P is defined as the dipole moment per unit volume V of a polarised material, P = . The SI unit is coulombs per square metre.

The rate at which electrical energy is supplied; or the rate at which electrical energy is dissipated in a system. For a direct current circuit, it is measured by the product of the current passing through a system and the potential difference across it: P = IV . In alternating-current circuits, the power is given by VI cosφ, where V and I are the RMS values and φ is the phase angle. Cosφ is called the power factor of the circuit. The SI unit of power is the watt and the term wattage is used to mean electric power in watts. Electricity can be produced mechanically by generation or chemically or by direct conversion from light in photovoltaic cells, also it can be stored chemically in batteries. When electric current flows in a circuit, it can transfer energy to do mechanical or thermodynamic work, with devices converting electrical energy into many useful forms, such as heat (electric heaters), light (light bulbs), motion (electric motors), sound (loudspeaker) or chemical changes. With resistive loads, Joule's law can be combined with Ohm's law ( $$I = \frac{V}{R}$$ ) to yield another equation for dissipated power: Given that R is the electrical resistance, then P= I2 R= V2 R .
A measure of the capacity of an electrical element to conduct current. It is the inverse quantity of electrical resistance with the symbol G and expressed as G = ,.

It is commonly represented by the Greek letter σ (sigma), but κ (kappa) (especially in electrical engineering) or γ (gamma) are also occasionally used. Its SI unit is siemens per metre (S ⋅ m^-1 ). It is expressed as σ = , where ρ is the resistivity. For a body of length L , resistance R and cross sectional area A , the electrical conductivity is given by σ = .

The flow of electric charges as current along a conductor or a circuit to create energy that is converted into other forms of energy. It is a form of power created by the movement of electrons. Electrical energy is a secondary source of energy, which is obtained through the conversion of other forms of energy known as the primary sources of energy. The primary sources from which electrical energy is obtained can be either non-renewable forms of energy or renewable forms of energy. Examples are hydro or water, coal, nuclear energy, natural gas, oil, wind, from chemical reactions as in cells or batteries, etc. Power, measured in watts and time measured in seconds are factors of electrical energy, expressed as: Energy = Power x Time. The unit of energy is the joule. In terms of the charge of electron, e and applied voltage, V , electrical energy, E can be expressed as E = eV . Therefore, electrical power that has been converted into work in a certain time or power that has been used over time is called electrical energy. Electrical energy is expressed in kilowatt-hour (kWhr): Power (kw) × time (hour).

Name for a scalar field, φ and a vector field, A, in terms of which the electric field and magnetic field, E and B respectively, may be expressed completely. This results in a degree of simplification in the use of Maxwell's equations, particularly in their relativistic formulation.

Electrons released from a hot cathode by thermionic emission, all moving through vacuum with the same acceleration from cathode to anode. The speed at which the electron arrive at the anode can be determined by equating the kinetic energy gained to electrical potential energy lost: 1 2 mv 2 = eV ; v = 2 eV m e , where m is the mass of electrons, e the electronic charge, v the speed of electrons and V is the potential difference across the terminals.

1. A radioactive transformation process for isotopes that have too many protons in the nucleus and insufficient energy to emit a positron. In this case, one of the orbital electrons, usually from the K or L shell is captured by a proton in nucleus, thus forming a neutron and a neutrino (neutral elementary particle). Since the proton is changed to a neutron the atomic number decreases by 1, the nuclide is transformed into a new element. But the atomic mass number remains unchanged. Examples of nuclides that undergo electron capture are 41 Ca, 51 Cr, 56 Ni, etc. 2. The formation of a negative ion by an atom or molecule when it acquires an extra free electron or a radioactive transformation in which a nucleus acquires an electron from an inner orbit of the atom thereby transforming initially into a nucleus with the same mass number but an atomic number one less than that of the original nucleus. It is accompanied by emission of an x-ray photon or Auger electron as the vacancy in the inner orbit is filled by an outer electron. If the energy difference between the parent atom and the daughter atom is less than 1.022 MeV, positron emission is forbidden and electron capture is the sole decay mode. For example, Rubidium^-83 will decay to Krypton^-83 only by electron capture (the energy difference is about 0.9 MeV).
Atomic fundamental physical constant used as atomic unit of mass. It symbol is m e , which is = 9.1093897 (54) x 10 -31 kg.

A chemical reaction that involves the addition of a molecule to an unsaturated organic compound across a double or triple bond. In this reaction, a π bond is broken and two new σ bonds are formed in a chemical compound. The sustaining force for this reaction is the formation of an electrophile X + that forms a covalent bond with an electron-rich unsaturated C=C bond. The positive charge on X is transferred to the carbon-carbon bond, with the formation of a carbocation.

The total number of electrons in an element is equal to the total number of protons, but the number of neutrons may be different. Elements are classified in families or groups in the periodic table and they are often classified also as metals and non-metals. A metallic element is one whose atoms form positive ions in a solution and a non-metallic element is one whose atoms form negative ions in a solution. Some of the elements, including oxygen, nitrogen, the noble gases (helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon), sulfur, copper, silver and gold are found in nature in the free (uncombined) state. Most of the elements in nature are combined with other elements in the form of compounds. The most abundant element on the Earth is oxygen and the most abundant element in the universe is hydrogen. 6. In electricity, the resistance wire in an electrical appliance such as an electric iron or oven.

Of models, such that every sentence in one model is true in the other. Two structures M and N of the same signature, σ are elementarily equivalent if every first-order sentence (formula without free variables) over σ is true in M if and only if it is true in N. This is a weaker relation than isomorphism; that is isomorphic models are elementarily equivalent, but not necessarily vice versa. For example, the non-standard real numbers and the ordinary real numbers are elementarily equivalent.

For example, log[tan^-1 [√(exp( x 2 ) + 1)] is constructed by successively applying each of the following operations to the result of the preceding: squaring, exponentiating, adding 1, extracting the square root, finding the inverse of the sine taking the logarithm. Assuming that the distance between two points R, R′ of a plane is denoted by 2 c , c > 0, let 2 a be a constant, with a > c . Then the ellipse with foci R and R ′ and major axis 2 a is the locus of points P of the plane such that PR + PR ′ = 2 a , where PF denotes the distance of P and R . One property of an ellipse is that the reflection offits boundary of a line from one focus will pass through the other. The standard equation of an ellipse is given by x 2 a 2 + y 2 b 2 = 1. 2. It is a closed type of quadric surface that is a higher dimensional analogue of an ellipse. The equation of a standard axis-aligned ellipsoid body in an xyz -Cartesian coordinate system is x 2 a 2 + y 2 b 2 + z 2 c 2 = 1, where, a and b are the equatorial radii along the x and y axes and c is the polar radius along the z -axis, all of which are fixed positive real determining the shape of the ellipsoid. Elliptic refers to possessing the shape of an ellipse; broad at the middle but narrowing at the two equal ends.

The set of solutions to a type of cubic equation whose solutions lie on a torus (a donut-shaped surface). The particular type of cubic equation whose solutions lead to elliptic curves takes the form: y 2 + axy + by = x 3 + cx 2 + dx + e .

In complex analysis, it is a function in which one of the forms expresses the relation of the arc of an ellipse to the straight lines to which it is connected. While a singly periodic function like sine has a number, a = 2 π , so that sin( x + a ) = sin( x ), a doubly periodic function f has the property that there are two numbers a , b , not rational multiples of each other, so that f ( x + a ) = f ( x + b ) = f ( x ).

A definite integral not usually evaluable in closed form by antidifferentiation, having the form R ( x , y ) c u ∫ dx, where R is a rational function of x and y , y 2 is a quartic polynomial in x and c is a fixed constant. It is a generalisation of the inverse trigonometric functions and provides solutions to more problems. Elliptic functions are obtained by inverting elliptic integrals to obtain generalisations of the trigonometric functions. The integral is called a complete elliptic integral if the range of integration is maximal; if not, it is an incomplete elliptic integral . The integral is named elliptic because one of the integrals expresses the length of an arc of an ellipse.

A paraboloid that can be put into a position such that its sections parallel to one coordinate plane are ellipses, while its sections parallel to the other two coordinate planes are parabolas. In other words, the vertical cross sections are all parabolas, while the horizontal cross sections are ellipses. In a suitable coordinate system with three axes x , y and z , it can be represented by the equation z c = x 2 a 2 + y 2 b 2 , where a and b are constants that dictate the level of curvature in the x - z and y - z planes respectively. With a = b an elliptic paraboloid is a paraboloid of revolution: a surface obtained by revolving a parabola around its axis. This is an elliptic paraboloid which opens upward for c > 0 and downward for c < 0. It is the shape of the parabolic reflectors used in mirrors, antenna dishes, etc.; and is also the shape of the surface of a rotating liquid, a principle used in liquid mirror telescopes and in making solid telescope mirrors.

The ability of a surface to emit radiation, measured as the ratio of the energy radiated by a surface to that radiated by a blackbody at the same temperature or the ratio of the radiation intensity of a nonblack body to the radiation intensity of a blackbody. Its symbol is ε. Its value is always less than or just equal to one. It varies with temperature and throughout the spectrum. Published values can readily be obtained for most substances.

The chemical formula showing the relative or simplest proportion of atoms of elements in a compound instead of their structural arrangement or molecular weights. For example, the formula HO is the empirical formula for H2 O2 , which means there is one H for every O atom. The empirical formula for ethanoic acid is CH2 O and it represents the atoms in their simplest whole number ratio. It makes no reference to isomerism, structure or absolute number of atoms and it is used as a standard for most ionic compounds, including CaCl 2 and for macromolecules, such as SiO2 . empirical formula of a compound is the formula which expresses only the relative number of atoms of each element in the compound. Empirical formulas are are obtained from experimental data and are useful to determine the molecular mass (or weight) of compounds whose molecular masses have not been known; and also to determine the molecular masses of compounds whose molecular masses are variable, even though they have a definite percentage composition (i.e., for different compounds formed from the same elements). On the other hand, the molecular formula gives types and numbers of atoms present, for example, the molecular formula for ethanoic acid is C2 H4 O2 . The structural formula indicates the way the atoms are arranged and it is commonly written by dividing the formula into groups. For example, ethanoic acid can be written as CH3 COOH. The structure can also be drawn to show how the elements are bonded or linked to one another.

A measure of the ratio of the relative weight of the brain of a particular species compared with the expected value for members of the group to which it belongs or that of a typical animal size. EQ = w(brain)/Ew(brain). The formula for the expected weight of the brain varies, but is usually Ew (brain) = 0.12w (body) 2/3 , though for some classes of animals the power is 3/4 rather than 2/3. The value is used to estimate the comparative intelligence of animals, particularly in anthropology. It is believed that the larger an organism is, the more brain weight is required for basic survival tasks such as breathing, thermoregulation, senses, motor skill, etc. The larger the brain is relative to the body, the more brain weight might be E available for more complex cognitive tasks. This method, as opposed to the method of simply measuring brain weight alone, puts humans closer at the top of the list. Also, reflecting the evolution of the recent cerebral cortex, different animals have different degrees of brain folding, which increase the surface of the cortex, which is positively correlated to intelligence in humans.

A chemical or biochemical reaction requiring an external source of free energy, which is usually heat or a reaction with a positive free energy change, in which case, energy is absorbed in the form of heat. Examples are photosynthesis, melting ice, cracking of alkanes, evaporation of water, thermal decomposition reactions, reaction of barium hydroxide octahydrate crystals with dry ammonium chloride, splitting a gas molecule apart and dissolving ammonium chloride in water. In endothermic reactions reaction, there is a loss in the total amount of energy; it takes more energy to start the reaction than what comes out of it, so that the total energy is a negative net result. Under constant temperature and pressure, the change in the standard Gibbs free energy would be positive for the reaction at standard pressure (1 bar) and standard concentrations (1 molar) of all the reagents. 1. The process of increasing the abundance of a specified isotope in a mixture of isotopes. In a nuclear reactor or weapon, it is normally applied to increase the proportion of U^-235 or the addition of Pu^-239 to natural uranium for use by the reactor. 2. In analytical chemistry, the process of increasing the concentration of trace components of a solution by preconcentration. Metal ions in natural waters can be enriched using cation exchange chromatography.

A thermodynamic property of a system denoted by H and defined by H=U+pV, where U is the internal energy of the system, p its pressure and V the volume. It is used to calculate the heat transferred during a quasi static process taking place in a closed thermodynamic system under constant pressure (isobaric process). In an endothermic reaction, the enthalpy change is positive, while it is negative in an exothermic reaction. It cannot be measured directly but when chemical substances react, the difference in the heat energy between the reactants and products can be measured. This difference E is the enthalpy change and is given by the symbol ∆H. Specific enthalpy is denoted as h Entire Leaf .

1. A measure of the unavailability of a system's energy to do work or a measure of the microscopic disorder within a system. An increase in entropy is accompanied by a decrease in energy available in a closed system. It is an important part of the second law of thermodynamics, which states that the thermodynamic entropy is a measure of the amount of energy which does no work during energy conversions. If thermodynamic systems are described using thermal energy instead of temperature, then entropy is just a number by which the thermal energy in the system is multiplied and the resulting energy is an energy for which no information is available, which would be required to convert the energy in technical systems from one form, for example, electrical into mechanical. A colourless, inflammable liquid with the molecular formula C2 H4 O, density 0.788 gcm^-3 , melting point^-123.5 °C (150 K) and a boiling point of 20.8 °C (293.95 K). It is a member of the group of organic compounds called aldehydes and it is formed by the oxidation of ethanol or ethane. It is produced by plants as part of their normal metabolism and it occurs naturally in ripe fruits, coffee and bread. It is also produced by oxidation of ethanol. It is an important precursor to pyridine derivatives, pentaerythritol and crotonaldehyde. It combines with urea to give a useful resin.

A colourless flammable liquid with a pungent odour and unpleasant taste having the chemical formula C6 H12 O3 , molar mass 132.16 g mol^-1 , melting point 12 °C (285 K) and boiling point 124 °C (397 K). It is produced by treating acetaldehyde with a small amount of sulfuric acid. It is slightly soluble in water and highly soluble in alcohol. It is used as a sedative and hypnotic drug (the safest hypnotic drug); in the manufacture of synthetic resins; as a preservative; and in preparing leather.

A colourless, odourless gas at standard temperature and pressure with the chemical formula C2 H6 , density 1.3562 mg cm^-3 (at 0 °C, 273.15 K) and 0.5446 g cm^-3 (at^-89.15 o C, 184 K), melting point^-183 °C (90.4 K) and boiling point^-89 °C (184.6 K). It is the second member of the alkane series of hydrocarbons (paraffins). It is isolated industrially from natural gas and as a by-product of petroleum refining. It is used as a plasticiser and as an industrial solvent, however, N,N-dimethylacetamide (DMA), which is a related compound is more widely used. It is also used as petrochemical feedstock for ethylene production. It is the only two-carbon alkane that is an aliphatic hydrocarbon.

A colourless, odourless, syrupy, sweet-tasting and viscous hygroscopic liquid, with the molecular formula C2 H6 O2 , molar mass, 62.07 g mol^-1 , density 1.1132 g/cm³, melting point^-12.9 °C (260 K) and boiling point 97.3°C (470 K). It is made by hydrolysis of epoxyethane from ethene and used as antifreeze and raw material for making polyesters. It is toxic and ingestion can result in death.

A colourless poisonous dicarboxylic acid, with the molecular formula H2 C2 O4 , density 1.90 gcm^-3 (anhydrous), 1.653 gcm^-3 (dihydrate) and melting point 189- 191°C (462-464 K). It typically occurs as a dihydrate with the chemical formula C2 O4 H2 ·2H2 O. It is obtained from plants or made synthetically. It is about 3,000 times stronger than acetic acid. Its conjugate base, known as oxalate (C2 O4 2- ), is a reducing agent as well as a chelating agent for metal cations. It is used for dyeing, bleaching and cleaning.

A colourless, poisonous liquid, with the chemical formula CH3 CN, density 0.787 g/ml liquid, melting point^-45 °C (228 K) and boiling point 82 °C (355 K). It is made by dehydrating ethanamide or from ammonia and ethyne. It is produced mainly as a by-product of acrylonitrile manufacture. It has a dipole moment of 3.84 D and it is a good polar solvent used for dissolving a wide range of ionic and nonpolar compounds when water cannot be used. In the laboratory, it is used as a medium-polarity solvent that is miscible with water and has a convenient liquid range. It is mainly used as a polar aprotic solvent in the purification of butadiene.

A liquid carboxylic acid with the chemical formula CH3 CO2 H, density 1.049 g cm^-3 , melting point 16-17 °C (289-290 K) and boiling point 118-119 °C (391-392 K), whose salts and esters are acetates. In its pure or glacial state, it is a clear, syrupy, corrosive liquid that mixes readily with water. It occurs naturally as a metabolic intermediate in body fluids and plant juices. Its dilute solution, from fermentation and oxidation of natural products is vinegar. Industrial production is either synthetic, from acetylene; or biological, from ethanol. Industrial chemicals made from it are used in printing and as plastics, photographic films, textiles and solvents.

A colourless liquid with a sharp, pungent odour. Its molecular formula is C4 H6 O3 , boiling point 139.8 °C (412.9 K) and a melting point of^-73.1 °C (200.1 K). It is produced by carbonylation of methyl acetate. It is mainly used in converting cellulose to cellulose acetate, a coating material used in the production of plastics, photographic film and fabrics. It is also used in the production of aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) and as a wood preservative. It can be safely used to substitute ethanoyl (acetyl) group (CH3 CO-) into organic compounds.

A colourless, limpid, volatile, flammable, toxic liquid with a pleasant odour and a pungent taste and the molecular formula C2 H5 OH, relative density 0.7851 at 20 °C, melting point at^-112.3 °C (160.85 K) and boiling point at 78.4°C (351.55 K). It is soluble in water and most organic liquids. It is produced by chemical synthesis and by fermentation or biosynthetic processes. It is the alcohol found in alcoholic drinks such as beer, wine and spirits. Apart from being a key input into alcoholic beverages, it is used as a solvent, extractant, antifreeze and intermediate in the synthesis of innumerable organic chemicals.

A colourless pungent liquid acid chloride with the chemical formula CH3 COCl, density 1.104 g/ml (liquid), melting point^-112 °C (161 K) and boiling point 52 °C (325 K). It is derived from acetic acid. It is made by reacting ethanoic acid with a halogenating agent such as phosphorus(III) chloride, phosphorus(V) chloride or sulfur dichloride oxide. It is used to introduce ethanoyl groups into organic compounds containing -OH, -NH2 and -SH groups. It does not exist in nature, because contact with water would hydrolyse it into acetic acid and hydrogen chloride.

A colourless, flammable, gaseous hydrocarbon with the molecular formula C2 H4, which is derived from natural gas and petroleum. It is the first member of the alkene series of hydrocarbons. It is made by cracking hydrocarbons from petroleum and is a major raw material for making other organic chemicals such as ethanal, ethanol and ethane^-1,2-diol. It can be polymerised to polyethene. It occurs naturally in plants, in which it acts as a growth substance. Its best-known effect is the stimulation of fruit ripening. Fruits such as bananas, apple and avocados naturally produce ethylene during the later stages of their ripening and ethylene gas is used to induce ripening in fruits, which are picked green. It also suppresses flowering, except in members of the pineapple family, where flowering may be synchronised by releasing ethylene into the growing plant. It is used as a source of many organic compounds, in welding and cutting metals, to colour citrus fruits and as an anaesthetic.

It is a primary amine made by reacting chloroethane with ammonia. It is used in petroleum refining, in detergents and in organic synthesis.

A colourless flammable liquid, with the chemical formula C6 H5 CH2 CH3 , density 0.8665 g/ml, melting point^-95 °C (178 K) and boiling point 136 °C (409 K). It is an aromatic hydrocarbon, whose greatest use (over 99 percent) is as an intermediate in the production of styrene monomer. It is also used as a solvent for coatings and in the production of synthetic rubber and cellulose acetate.

The average outcome over a large number of repetitions of a random experiment. In other words, it is an average over infinitely many repetitions. A second-order linear differential equation whose coefficients are periodic single-valued functions of an independent variable x has a solution of the form e μx P ( x ), where μ is a constant and P ( x ) a periodic function.

A symbolic representation of the structure of a flower using specific letters, numbers and symbols. Each kind of floral part is represented by the letter K for calyx, C for corolla, P for perianth, A for androecium, G for gynoecium and a number to indicate the quantity of the part present, for example, C5 for a flower with five petals. It also indicates whether the ovary is inferior or superior.

It relates quantities in equilibrium and non-equilibrium statistical mechanics and microscopic and macroscopic quantities. The principle underlying this theorem is that a non-equilibrium state may have been reached either as a result of a random fluctuation or an external force such as an electric or magnetic field and that the evolution towards equilibrium is the same in both cases. The fluctuation-dissipation theorem enables transport coefficients to be calculated in terms of response to external fields.

A chemically reactive, poisonous, gaseous element in Group 17 (VIIA) elements in the Periodic Table. Its chemical symbol is F, atomic number 9, atomic weight 18.9984, freezing point^-219.62 °C (53.53 K), melting point^-223 °C (50 K) and boiling point^-188.14 °C (85 K), specific gravity of liquid 1.108 (at boiling point) and valence 1. It is the most chemically active nonmetallic element and the most electronegative of all the elements. Its chief source is fluorite. It also occurs in cryolite, fluorapatite, seawater, bones and teeth. Hydrogen fluoride (HF) is a raw material for many other fluorides. It can be produced only by electrolysis under special conditions. It is an essential trace element needed for the healthy development of bones and teeth and to prevent tooth decay. Fluorine compound, fluorite is used as a flux in refining iron; another compound, cryolite serves as the electrolyte in the production of aluminium. Compounds of fluorine are also used in the ceramic and glass industries. Hydrofluoric acid is used to etch glass and in the manufacture of light bulbs. Sodium fluoride (NaF) is added to water and tin fluoride (SnF2 ) to dental-care products to reduce dental caries.

Any influence (push or pull) that causes an object to accelerate, slowdown or change shape or any influence that tends to change the state of rest or the uniform motion in the straight line of a body. A force has both magnitude and direction, making it a vector quantity; and expressed as Force = mass x acceleration. Its symbol is F and the unit is the Newton (N), defined as the force required to cause a mass of one kilogram to accelerate at a rate of one meter per second squared in the absence of other force-producing effects which is equal to 1 kg m/s 2 .

A value which is unique to a bond which characterises the strength of the bond in a diatomic molecule. The force constant is a measure of the resistance offered to stretching and vibration of a bond, the magnitude of which indicates how strongly the atoms are held together and hence stability.

Some formal systems, such as Euclidean geometry, are built around a few basic axioms and can be expanded with theorems that can be deduced through proofs.

A toxic colourless gaseous compound belonging to the family of organic compounds called aldehydes. Its chemical formula is CH2 O, density 0.8153 g/cm³ (-20°C, 253 K), melting point^-92°C (181 K) and a boiling point of^-19°C (254 K). It is used for manufacturing melamine and phenolic resins, fertilisers, dyes and embalming fluids and in aqueous solution as a preservative and disinfectant.

The equilibrium constant for the formation of a complex ion from its components in solution. It is a measure of the strength of the interaction between the reagents that come together to form the complex.

The parent compound H2 NN=CHN=NH and its derivatives formed by substitution at carbon and/or nitrogen.

For example, A = πr 2 is the formula for calculating the area of a circle; and C = πD , expresses the relationship between the circumference and diameter of a circle. 2. A formal expression of some rule or other result, for example, Stirling's formula or Frenet formulae. 3. A representation of a molecule, ion or radical in which the compound's chemical elements are represented by the chemical symbol. 4. Functions within computer programs often contain formulas, which are used to process data that is passed through the function and output the result. A section in Microsoft Excel and other spreadsheets that displays the data or formula stored in the active cell and allows users to enter formulas instead of static data. In Microsoft Excel, it is located above the work area of the spreadsheet.

The lowest reduced ratio of ions in a compound. It is the empirical formula of an ionic or covalent network compound used as an independent entity for stoichiometric calculations. Examples include ionic sodium chloride (NaCl), Potassium oxide (K2 O) and covalent networks such as silicon dioxide (SiO2 ) and C (as diamond or graphite).

The sum of the atomic weights of all atoms in a molecule. The term is generally applied to a substance that consists of ions rather than individual molecules. An example of such a substance is sodium chloride (NaCl). Such a substance's chemical formula describes the simplest ratio of the number of atoms of the constituent elements.

1. Putting together of components in appropriate relationships or structures, according to a formula. 2. The particular mixture of base chemicals and additives required for a product. In pharmacy, it is a mixture or a structure such as a capsule, a pill, tablet or an emulsion, prepared according to a specific procedure. 3. Formulation science is concerned with the knowledge and practice of blending and mixing of various components (chemical molecules) in a way that they do not react, but interact to provide a final product with very specific desirable properties or functions. Formulation science covers the core of physical and colloid chemistries, as well as analytical chemistry, chemical engineering, pharmaceutical and biological sciences.

A colourless volatile sweet-smelling liquid haloform with the chemical formula CHCl 3 , relative density 1.48, melting point^-63.5 °C (209.5 K) and boiling point 61.7 °C (334.7 K). It can be made by chlorination of methane followed by separation of the mixture of products or by the haloform reaction. It is an effective anaesthetic but can cause liver damage and it has now been replaced by other halogenated hydrocarbons. It is used as a solvent and raw material for making other compounds.

The theorem that any planar map can be coloured using at most four colours in such a way that no two adjacent areas are of the same colour. Two American mathematicians, Kenneth Ira Appel (1932-2013) at the University of Illinois and his colleague Wolfgang Haken (1928 - ) provided a mathematical proof in 1978 that solved the long-standing four-colour map problem.

An empirical law based on observation. It states that the rate of heat flow, dQ/dt, through a homogeneous solid is directly proportional to the area, A, of the section at right angles to the direction of heat flow and to the temperature difference along the path of heat flow, dT/dx .

The subgroup, Φ(G), of a given group G defined to be the intersection of all maximal subgroups of G. If G has no maximal subgroups, its Frattini subgroup is defined as Φ(G) = G.

It is named in honour of German physicist, Heinrich Rudolf Hertz (1857 - 1894). The unit of frequency (f) is the hertz (Hz), which is equal to 1 cycle per second (1/s). Its symbol is Hz. It is expressed as f = ω/2π, where f is the frequency of the vibrating article and ω is the angular speed.

For a constrained minimisation, one adds an additional non-negative multiplier, λ 0 , for the objective function and asserts that not all the multipliers are simultaneously zero. A constraint qualification can be viewed as ensuring that λ 0 is nonzero and so can be scaled to unity.

The theorem states that every polynomial equation having complex coefficients and degree ≥ 1 has at least one complex root. This theorem was first proven by Gauss. It is equivalent to the statement that a polynomial P ( z ) of degree n has n values z i (some of them possibly degenerate) for which P ( z i ) = 0. Such values are called polynomial roots. The theorem stating that any positive integer can be expressed as a unique product of prime numbers.

A theorem that links the concept of the derivative of a function with the concept of the integral. The first part of the theorem, sometimes called the first fundamental theorem of calculus is that an indefinite integration can be reversed by a differentiation. This part of the theorem is also important because it guarantees the existence of antiderivatives for continuous functions. The second part, sometimes called the second fundamental theorem of calculus states that the definite integral of a function can be computed by using any one of its infinitely many antiderivatives. This part of the theorem has key practical applications because it markedly simplifies the computation of definite integrals.

It is prepared commercially by dehydration of pentose sugars obtained from cornstalks and corncobs, husks of oat and peanut and other waste products. It is used as a solvent for extracting mineral oils and natural resins and by itself forms resins with some aromatic compounds. It is also used in the manufacture of pesticides, phenolfurfural resins and tetrahydrofuran.
